Watching Manuel Neuer finally save the opponent’s fifth penalty to keep Germany alive, only for Jonathan Tah to blast our sixth penalty over the bar, was absolutely heartbreaking. Three consecutive World Cups, three early exits. Even Germany’s once-unbeaten World Cup penalty shootout record has finally come to an end.

I became a Germany fan back in 2002 because of Miroslav Klose’s iconic headed goals and front-flips, Michael Ballack’s warrior spirit, and Oliver Kahn’s commanding presence. I’ve supported Germany ever since. Watching that German machine evolve from 2002 to finally lifting the World Cup in 2014 was an unforgettable journey. Their football was smooth, disciplined, and consistently brilliant. Even when they lost, you could still admire the way they played.

Now Germany has two extraordinary talents in Florian Wirtz and Jamal Musiala—the so-called “€100 million twin stars”—yet the team’s overall performances have been deeply disappointing.

By the final whistle, I couldn’t help but feel that Neuer probably shouldn’t have returned to the national team. At nearly 40, time has finally caught up with him. It was painful to witness the last remaining member of that legendary generation of the German machine bow out in such a cruel fashion.

From 2002 to 2014, that Germany side repeatedly eliminated Lionel Messi’s Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal, and even England—whose Frank Lampard should have had that famous goal awarded. They conquered so many of the world’s biggest footballing powers.

Last World Cup, I witnessed Messi finally fulfil his dream of becoming a world champion. This time, I hope either Cristiano Ronaldo achieves his dream, or football finally comes home with England lifting the trophy. Those legendary rivals were part of what made that great German team so unforgettable.

Ironically, with Italy—once Germany’s biggest World Cup nemesis—missing three consecutive tournaments, Germany themselves have now suffered three straight early exits. Football truly is unpredictable.

The fluent, direct attacking football combined with the legendary German fighting spirit of that era is gone. My disappointment with Germany from 2018 to 2026 runs so deep precisely because I was fortunate enough to witness—and passionately support—that unforgettable Germany team from 2002 to 2014, which will always remain my favourite.

Watching Manuel Neuer finally save the opponent’s fifth penalty to keep Germany alive, only for Jonathan Tah to blast our sixth penalty over the bar, was absolutely heartbreaking. Three consecutive World Cups, three early exits. Even Germany’s once-unbeaten World Cup penalty shootout record has finally come to an end.

I became a Germany fan back in 2002 because of Miroslav Klose’s iconic headed goals and front-flips, Michael Ballack’s warrior spirit, and Oliver Kahn’s commanding presence. I’ve supported Germany ever since. Watching that German machine evolve from 2002 to finally lifting the World Cup in 2014 was an unforgettable journey. Their football was smooth, disciplined, and consistently brilliant. Even when they lost, you could still admire the way they played.

Now Germany has two extraordinary talents in Florian Wirtz and Jamal Musiala—the so-called “€100 million twin stars”—yet the team’s overall performances have been deeply disappointing.

By the final whistle, I couldn’t help but feel that Neuer probably shouldn’t have returned to the national team. At nearly 40, time has finally caught up with him. It was painful to witness the last remaining member of that legendary generation of the German machine bow out in such a cruel fashion.

From 2002 to 2014, that Germany side repeatedly eliminated Lionel Messi’s Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal, and even England—whose Frank Lampard should have had that famous goal awarded. They conquered so many of the world’s biggest footballing powers.

Last World Cup, I witnessed Messi finally fulfil his dream of becoming a world champion. This time, I hope either Cristiano Ronaldo achieves his dream, or football finally comes home with England lifting the trophy. Those legendary rivals were part of what made that great German team so unforgettable.

Ironically, with Italy—once Germany’s biggest World Cup nemesis—missing three consecutive tournaments, Germany themselves have now suffered three straight early exits. Football truly is unpredictable.

The fluent, direct attacking football combined with the legendary German fighting spirit of that era is gone. My disappointment with Germany from 2018 to 2026 runs so deep precisely because I was fortunate enough to witness—and passionately support—that unforgettable Germany team from 2002 to 2014, which will always remain my favourite.

Great video! For me, the definition of a dark horse is a "good team" that is NOT one of the historical winners nor one of the historical contenders (ex. the Netherlands). Any team not within those limits is considered a dark horse as long as they have gone further than they were expected to AND (inevitably, taken the heads of at least one of the above categories of teams). 

Someone made a great observation that it often means that that team is from the continent that the WC is hosted on, but i think thats only been true for the last couple of editions. In Mexico 86, Denmark was considered the dark horse, for example. In Italia 90, it was Cameroon. In 94, arguably Bulgaria. 

Ironically, in 2010 I would say Uruguay was the dark horse, despite them being part of the winners club. But lets face it, they are the outliers of this definition, not having been true contenders for 80 years.

Honest answer, yes and no. Yes, Ronaldo may be part of the problem. But no, simply replacing him will not solve it. You could put Harry Kane in that position and he would probably still struggle to receive the ball consistently. and then service others that do not attack the open space. 
Portugal has a recurring problem against teams that defend compactly. The issue is not solely the striker, but the structure behind him. Against this type of opponent, Martínez probably needs to leave out one of Portugal’s “sacred midfielders”, namely Vitinha, João Neves, Bruno Fernandes or Bernardo Silva. As someone in the Portuguese media put it, Martínez seems mentally hostage to these players because he always tries to fit all of them into the same team. Over the past year, this has led to João Neves playing at right-back, where he does reasonably well but is far from ideal, and to Fernandes or Bernardo being used in wide positions that do not fully provide what Portugal need from those areas. Bernardo can play on the right, but he naturally comes inside and helps control possession. Against a compact defence, Portugal often need someone more direct, capable of attacking the defensive line and providing forward progression. Against a team like Congo, that could mean using Trincão, Francisco Conceição, Félix as a second forward, or perhaps Leão from the left, even though he had a poor season. As much as I, as a Benfica fan, do not like Ronaldo, replacing him with Gonçalo Ramos or another striker is not enough on its own. Ramos may offer more pressing, movement and runs behind the defence, but he can still end up isolated between three centre-backs if the players behind him continue circulating the ball without progressing into dangerous areas. That is exactly what happened in the recent game against Mexico. 
Against Congo, Portugal controlled possession, attempted almost 800 passes, more than 500 of them sideways or backwards, and still struggled to involve the striker or create enough danger in the final third. Too much of the circulation took place outside the areas where any centre-forward could realistically receive the ball. The striker can drop back to become involved, but then Portugal end up with the same problem from the opposite direction, as there is nobody ahead of him to receive the next pass. 
This has been a recurring problem under Martínez. It has also appeared in matches where Ronaldo did not play, with his replacement facing the same basic issue because the ball rarely reached him in useful positions.

This whole debate about the tournament being "diluted" or "vulgar" is just institutional elitism disguised as concern for quality. Pundits love to protect the pre-established order of the 80s and 90s, but football history constantly disproves this myth of permanent European/South American superiority. 

Let's look at the actual facts:

1. "Elite" pedigree guarantees nothing on the pitch. We've seen reigning world champions Spain get dismantled 5-1 and exit in the group stage in 2014. We've watched Italy—a 4-time world champion and Euro 2020 winner—miss three consecutive World Cups. Yet, traditional giants like Uruguay can turn up, play terribly, and escape this harsh criticism based on "tradition" alone. 

2. Inclusion is what drives global quality. Critics said the exact same things when the tournament expanded to include more African teams decades ago. Fast forward to today: CAF teams absolutely crushed the group stage with an incredible 90% success rate, sending 9 out of 10 teams into the Round of 32. 

3. The African footprint is driving UEFA's success anyway. If you subtract the actual African nations, the top European sides left are completely anchored by the African diaspora—France has 18 players of African origin, Switzerland has 9, England has 8, and Germany has 7. 

Don is spot on here. You cannot expect smaller or developing football nations to magically build elite infrastructure and match sharpness if you try to lock the gates and deny them the pitch. We saw the exact same protectionist pushback with the Club World Cup expansion. Opening the doors to the world doesn't dilute the World Cup; it finally makes it a true World Cup. 🌍🏆

original_text: I’m as disappointed about not getting out the group as anyone, and I wanted Scotland to make more of a go of it but Reality check: 1) we weren’t qualifying for tournaments before Steve Clarke. I remember similar shouts about Craig Brown before we sacked him, and I said to my friends ‘be careful what you wish for’ and look what happened. History could well repeat itself and it’ll be another 30yrs before we’re going to tournaments. Let’s hope we don’t get another Berti Vogts next. 2) You can only pick the players you’ve got. We’re talking about wanting more goals, but our goal scorers are our midfielders (McTominay and McGinn) just look at the stats. Our forwards are English Championship Standard at best, our centre backs aren’t world class either. It’s nothing personal against these guys, it’s just their level and they were up against higher level players from Brazil and Morocco this tournament. You’re asking a lot from our midfield to defend providing an effective screen against that sort of opposition, whilst expecting them to be our main goal threat also. 3) Individual errors by players on the day, and dodgy decisions by officials also cost us but these things happen and can’t be accounted for by the manager. On another day we get at least one penalty vs Morocco and they also get a red card, and our defence don’t lose the ball to world class strikers in the box vs Brazil. Those decisions go our way, we’re in the next round and we’re having a different conversation. 4) as Mark McGhee said, you can predict before the tournament we’d likely lose to Morocco and Brazil, to margins that roughly add up to -4 goal difference (depending how each game went) and you’d accept that. Why the surprise when it happened? Aye we needed more goal against Haiti, but from where? You can’t go out and buy world class players at international level, you need to produce them. As Ian Wright said, someone somewhere at the SFA is letting the nation down in terms of developing our game/players. Aye we’re a small nation, our leagues something like 25th in terms of wealth in the world (England Premier league is top, and Championship 10th), but other small nations like Holland and Belgium do much better than us. Teams with poorer leagues than us eg Croatia, also consistently do better than us in terms of producing players and national team performance at tournaments. The problem is at a much higher level than our national team manager. Would I have selected a slightly different squad, yes, but only by a couple of players and it’s ultimately fringe players (not starters) people argue about in-terms of whether they should have made a squad or not. The bottom line is we’re disappointed because there was an opportunity, and we didn’t have a proper go at it. Steve Clark’s taken criticism but is that responsibility solely on the manager? Or is it a combination of a manager trying to do the best with what he’s got, and what he’s got isn’t as good as what he’s up against in conjunction with 50/50 game day decisions from officials not going our way? At club level, fans would be singing to sack the board after long periods of perceived under performance,  why are we not holding those in higher positions to account?
